subtype: Approach: watching a friend who rides well and copying [Action]
passage:
Monday: Aparna sat on the building steps with her chin on her knees and watched Alka from the third floor ride out. She noticed three things. Alka lifted one pedal high before starting. She pushed down hard on it to get going. And she never looked at her wheel, only at the gate.
Wednesday: Aparna wheeled her own cycle out and whispered the steps. "Pedal up. Push. Eyes on the gate." She rode four metres before she wobbled, then six.
Saturday: She knocked on Alka's door. "Will you watch me and tell me what's wrong?" Alka watched two rounds. "You push, then you stop pedalling. Keep going." Aparna kept going, all the way to the gate.

qa.q: What were the three steps Aparna whispered on Wednesday?
qa.a: She whispered "Pedal up. Push. Eyes on the gate."

qa.q: Why did Aparna knock on Alka's door on Saturday?
qa.a: She wanted help to spot her mistakes; she felt hopeful and trusted Alka enough to ask to be watched.

qa.q: What else could help Aparna if she still stops pedalling, and why?
qa.a: She could count her pedal turns aloud, because counting keeps her legs moving without thinking about the fall.

qa.q: How might Alka see being asked for help?
qa.a: Alka is probably pleased and a little proud to be asked, and her quick tip shows she is happy to help.

grounding: It shows a girl watching a neighbour's start, copying the steps one by one and then asking the neighbour to correct her.

subtype: Approach: watching a friend who rides well and copying [Action]
passage: Vaibhav, you keep asking how your Payal Mausi learnt to ride without anyone teaching her. Nobody had time to teach me, that's how. But there was Rosy next door, who rode to the milk booth every morning. So I became her shadow. I sat on our wall and watched her feet. Right pedal up, like a clock at two. One strong push. Head up, looking far down the road, never at the wheel. I copied one thing at a time on my brother's old cycle. First the pedal, then the push. Fell plenty. Then one day I swallowed my pride and asked Rosy, "Watch me, tell me what I'm doing wrong." She laughed and said, "You look down at the last second." That one sentence fixed it.

qa.q: Where did young Payal sit to watch Rosy?
qa.a: Young Payal sat on the wall and watched Rosy's feet.

qa.q: How did young Payal feel about asking Rosy for help?
qa.a: Young Payal felt shy and a bit proud, having to swallow that pride before asking to be watched.

qa.q: What turning point in the story made the biggest difference, and why?
qa.a: The turning point was asking Rosy to watch, because Rosy could spot the look-down mistake that Payal could not see alone.

qa.q: How might Rosy have felt when the girl from next door asked for help?
qa.a: Rosy was probably amused and pleased, and happy to share the one tip that fixed it.

grounding: An elder recalls how, as a girl, she watched a neighbour ride, copied the steps one at a time and asked the neighbour to correct her.

subtype: Approach: setting small goals such as ten metres, then twenty [Revision]
passage:
"I'm stuck, Chandrika didi. I get three metres and fall. Every time."
"Every time? Let's check." She picked up a stick of chalk from the rangoli box. "Here's your start line. Here, ten big steps away, a line. That's ten metres, roughly."
"Ten? I can't do ten."
"Then fall and try again. I'll mark where you put your foot down."
Omkar rode. Fell. She drew a small cross. Rode again. Another cross, a little further.
"Didi, that one's past the last one!"
"And that one's past that."
By dinner, six crosses crept toward the line and one sat right on it.
"Tomorrow," Omkar said, "draw the twenty line."

qa.q: What did Chandrika use to mark where Omkar put his foot down?
qa.a: She used a stick of chalk from the rangoli box to draw a small cross.

qa.q: How did Omkar feel when he saw a cross past the last one?
qa.a: He felt excited and encouraged, because he could see he was getting further even though he still fell.

qa.q: What other approach could help Omkar after reaching twenty, and why?
qa.a: He could try riding a curve around a flowerpot, because a new small target keeps practice interesting once distance feels easy.

qa.q: How does the chalk plan look to Chandrika?
qa.a: Chandrika sees it as an easy way to show Omkar his progress, and she is probably glad to see his mood change.

grounding: It shows a boy who feels stuck at a few metres using chalk marks and ten- and twenty-metre goals to see his progress.

subtype: Approach: setting small goals such as ten metres, then twenty [Revision]
passage: For a whole week I thought I was hopeless at cycling. I'd ride a few metres, wobble and put a foot down. Always the same, I thought. Then on Saturday I took the chalk from my school bag and drew a line across our lane, ten metres from the gate. I said to myself, forget riding forever, just reach the line. First try, no. Fourth try, yes. So I drew another line, twenty metres. My sister Uma counted for me from the gate: "Yusuf, twelve! Fifteen! Eighteen!" I fell a lot. But every fall was further along, and I could see it on the road. On Monday I passed twenty. My knees are scraped, but I'm not hopeless any more.

subtype: Approach: repeating the list aloud again and again [Action]
passage: On Thursday Mrs. Rao said we needed seven things for Friday's craft class: glue, scissors, chart paper, crayons, cotton, ribbon and glitter. I didn't have a pencil, so I made them into a chant. Glue-scissors-chart-crayons-cotton-ribbon-glitter. I chanted it through the school gate and down the lane, over and over, like a song on a bus. It worked, until our front door. My little brother Mohit jumped out shouting, "Trisha didi, look, I lost a tooth!" I looked. I admired the tooth. When I opened my mouth to tell Amma the list, only five things came out. Ribbon and cotton had run away. On Friday I sat with a cotton-less, ribbon-less cloud picture.

subtype: Approach: making a funny sentence from the first letters [Thinking]
passage: Dhruv sits next to me, Amandeep, in Class 5, and on Tuesday he was muttering during break. "My. Very. Eager. Monkey. Just. Sat. Upon. Nani." I asked if he'd gone mad. He showed me his rough page. Down one side: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. Across: the silly sentence. "Each first letter is a planet," he said. "I can't remember eight names in a row. But I can see a monkey sitting on Nani. The monkey pulls the next word along." He was grinning like he'd found a secret door. On Friday Sharma sir asked the class for the planets in order. Dhruv's hand went up first, and I saw his lips move, just a little, before he answered.

Diary, today Madam said we need four things for Friday's trip to the bird park: a cap, a water bottle, a lunch box and something else. Everyone was writing. I didn't. I thought, four things, easy, I'm not a baby. At dinner Amma asked me and I said, "Cap, bottle, lunch box and..." and nothing came. I counted on my fingers. Three. The fourth one was just gone. I felt so stupid. Amma gave me her phone to call Neelam. It rang and rang. Her mother finally picked up and said Neelam was at her cousin's wedding. So now it's ten o'clock and I still don't know. Next time I write it.

Anjali had a list of eight things to bring for Wednesday's model-making class. I asked her to read it once, then close her notebook and tell me. She said six. She peeked, covered it again. Eight. She did it twice more until she could say all eight three times without a mistake. At the end she said, "I'll say it once before sleeping." Today she came with all eight things. I have started using her cover-and-say trick with the younger group.

grounding: It shows a girl who missed items testing herself by covering the list and repeating until she can say all of it, then sleeping on it.
